clinicalPearls: Characterised by sudden, recurrent, self-limiting attacks of arthritis and periarthritis lasting hours to a few days with complete resolution between episodes
Attacks typically affect one or a few joints at a time, most often the fingers, wrists and knees, sometimes with periarticular soft-tissue swelling
Crucially, there is no permanent joint damage or radiographic erosion despite recurrent flares
A significant proportion of patients, particularly those seropositive for rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibodies, progress to established rheumatoid arthritis
Anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor positivity are the strongest predictors of evolution to persistent inflammatory arthritis
Diagnosis rests on the characteristic history since patients are often asymptomatic with normal examination and imaging when reviewed between attacks
Colchicine, hydroxychloroquine and NSAIDs are used to reduce attack frequency, and DMARDs are considered when progression to rheumatoid arthritis is likely
reference.pathophysiology: Palindromic rheumatism is an episodic inflammatory arthropathy in which transient synovial and periarticular inflammation produces recurrent short-lived attacks without cumulative joint destruction. It is widely regarded as an abortive or early form of rheumatoid arthritis, and autoantibodies such as rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are frequently present, reflecting shared autoimmune mechanisms. During attacks there is neutrophil-rich synovial inflammation that resolves without pannus formation or erosion, but persistent autoimmunity in seropositive individuals can eventually give way to sustained synovitis and conversion to established rheumatoid arthritis or, less often, other connective tissue disease.
additionalDifferentials: Familial Mediterranean fever and other autoinflammatory syndromes
Systemic lupus erythematosus with intermittent arthritis
additionalInvestigations: Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies to stratify the risk of progression to rheumatoid arthritis
Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), often raised during attacks and normal between them
Joint radiographs, characteristically normal without erosions
Ultrasound during an attack to confirm synovitis and periarticular inflammation
Serum urate and joint aspiration to exclude crystal arthropathy when relevant
redFlags: Development of persistent rather than self-limiting joint swelling suggesting evolution to rheumatoid arthritis
Emergence of radiographic erosions indicating a destructive arthropathy
Systemic features (rash, serositis, cytopenias) pointing to lupus or another connective tissue disease
Fever with monoarthritis where septic or crystal arthritis must be excluded
reference.prognosis: Between attacks patients are usually asymptomatic with no lasting joint damage, but a substantial proportion, especially those with positive autoantibodies, progress to rheumatoid arthritis or another chronic inflammatory disease over time.
pitfalls: Dismissing the diagnosis because examination and imaging are normal between attacks
Failing to check autoantibodies and therefore missing patients at high risk of progression to rheumatoid arthritis
Confusing recurrent attacks with gout without joint aspiration or urate measurement
Delaying DMARD consideration in seropositive patients with frequent flares
